Upsidedown catfish (Synodontis batensoda) is a moderately sized mochokid species of West African freshwaters, and its maximum reported length provides a useful first metric for understanding its growth trajectory. Individuals attain an ultimate total length of 28.6 centimeters [Li = 28.6 centimeters], a value that places the species among the smaller to medium-sized members of the genus Synodontis. This asymptotic size is derived from field surveys of large adult specimens and serves as an important benchmark for life-history comparisons. Morphometric data indicate that the onset of reproductive capability occurs well before the fish reaches this maximum dimension, a pattern common among iteroparous tropical fishes. The body mass associated with the ultimate length has been estimated from length-weight regressions developed for congeners, providing an approximation of the maximum somatic size a fully grown individual can achieve. Such measurements are critical for parameterizing growth models and for assessing the ecological role of this species within its floodplain and riverine habitats, where seasonal food availability can influence both growth rates and the timing of maturation.

Reproduction in Synodontis batensoda is characterized by a strategy that balances fecundity against the constraints of a tropical thermal regime, and the species’ maximum reproductive output offers insight into its life-history tempo. At a water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], individual females produce approximately 264 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 264 eggs per day], reflecting a rate of gamete production that is considerable for a fish of this body size. This daily oviposition rate represents the peak reproductive potential under optimal conditions, though actual output in the wild likely varies with food availability and female condition. When expressed over a full breeding season, this daily fecundity implies a substantial total annual investment in offspring. The high rate is consistent with patterns observed in other mochokid catfishes from similar environments, where extended spawning periods allow for the continuous production of relatively small, planktonic eggs. Such a strategy maximizes the number of progeny that can be dispersed during favourable hydrological conditions, thereby increasing the likelihood that at least some offspring will encounter suitable nursery habitats.

The early life stages of the Upsidedown catfish are defined by a brief embryonic period and a remarkably small neonatal mass, both of which reflect the species’ reproductive ecology. At a stable incubation temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the interval from egg fertilisation to eclosion lasts approximately 9 days [ab = approximately 9 days], a duration typical of tropical catfishes with small, pelagic eggs that develop rapidly. Upon hatching, the yolk-sac larvae weigh approximately 0.00052 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00052 grams], an extremely low birth mass that underscores the energy-poor, high-fecundity strategy employed by this species. This minute wet weight at birth is derived from egg diameter measurements of a related congener and reflects the limited maternal investment per offspring. The newly emerged prolarvae are consequently dependent on rapid yolk absorption and the timely onset of exogenous feeding to sustain growth during the critical transition from endotrophic to exotrophic nutrition. The combination of a short incubation period and minimal birth mass suggests a strong selective pressure for high fecundity to offset high larval mortality in the unpredictable floodplain environments this species occupies.

Body mass at the onset of reproductive maturity provides a key marker for understanding the energetic threshold that triggers gonadal development in Synodontis batensoda. Individuals attain sexual maturity at a relatively modest size, with the corresponding wet weight at puberty estimated at 25 grams [Wwp = 25 grams], based on length-weight relationships derived from empirical data for this genus. This value indicates that females typically begin vitellogenesis and enter the spawning population well before they have reached their full somatic growth potential. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight, or maximum adult body mass recorded for the species, is approximately 242 grams [Wwi = approximately 242 grams], reflecting the considerable post-maturation growth that continues throughout the adult phase. This nearly tenfold increase in mass from the pubertal stage to the asymptotic size suggests that the species allocates substantial resources to continued somatic investment even after the initiation of reproductive activity. Such a pattern is common among iteroparous fishes in seasonal environments, where early reproduction is balanced against the long-term benefits of reaching a larger body size that confers higher fecundity and competitive advantage.

Longevity and overall life-history timing in Synodontis batensoda are further illuminated by lifespan data and comparisons with closely related species. The maximum recorded lifespan for this Upsidedown catfish, under captive conditions maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], is approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years], a duration that aligns with estimates for other similarly sized mochokids. This lifespan is long enough to facilitate multiple reproductive seasons, reinforcing the iteroparous life-history strategy inferred from its growth and fecundity patterns. The total length at which puberty is reached, measured at 13 centimeters [Lp = 13 centimeters], provides a morphological benchmark that, when viewed alongside the 9 day embryonic period at 25 °C and the 0.00052 gram birth mass, depicts a life cycle characterized by rapid early development, early maturation at a moderate body size, and a sustained period of adult growth and reproduction over nearly a decade. Taken together, these life-history traits paint a picture of a species well-adapted to the variable and productive conditions of tropical African river systems.
